summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for accord_glycemia, grouped by per-hypothesis feature attribution.

mechanisms.description: Assignment to the intensive glycemic‑control strategy (target HbA1c <6.0%) increases the incidence of trial‑adjudicated severe hypoglycemia, which mediates part of the observed excess all‑cause mortality.
Greater achieved HbA1c reduction under the intensive strategy mediates a reduction in MACE for a subset of participants who can safely attain lower glycemia.
A history of prior severe hypoglycemia predisposes participants randomized to intensive control to recurrent severe hypoglycemia, which in turn increases their risk of subsequent mortality.

Higher baseline HbA1c magnifies the degree of achievable HbA1c lowering under intensive assignment and therefore increases the likelihood of individualized MACE benefit compared with those with lower baseline HbA1c.

Higher baseline albuminuria marks participants who derive different cardiovascular benefit/harm balances from intensive control, with albuminuria modifying the mediated effect via achieved glycemic change or hypoglycemia.

Differential adherence and treatment crossovers dilute ITT estimates so that per‑protocol/CACE analyses reveal that the causal effect of actually achieved intensive glycemic intensity on outcomes operates through achieved HbA1c and hypoglycemia pathways.

Era and background therapy composition (trial‑era medications vs contemporary SGLT2i/GLP‑1 RA use) alter the causal pathway such that the net effect of intensive assignment on mortality and MACE is transportable only after accounting for these treatment‑era modifiers.

More intensive visit cadence and medication intensification behaviors (as captured in the emulated intensive‑like definitions) change monitoring and management of hypoglycemia, thereby modifying the observed incidence of severe hypoglycemia and subsequent outcome risks.

Baseline prior cardiovascular disease modifies the intensive versus standard treatment effect such that participants with prior CVD experience less net cardiovascular benefit and greater net harm from intensive control.
Reduced baseline kidney function (lower eGFR/advanced CKD stage) amplifies the risk of severe hypoglycemia under intensive control, thereby increasing mortality and offsetting any MACE benefit.

Baseline insulin use interacts with randomized assignment so that participants on insulin under the intensive strategy have higher severe hypoglycemia rates and different achieved HbA1c trajectories that alter net benefit/harm.
Longer diabetes duration attenuates the potential MACE reduction from intensive glycemic lowering while simultaneously increasing susceptibility to harms from intensive control.
Elevated baseline systolic blood pressure modifies the effect of intensive glycemic control on MACE and mortality, producing heterogeneous absolute risk differences across blood‑pressure strata.
Older age amplifies vulnerability to harms from intensive glycemic assignment, producing larger absolute increases in mortality or severe hypoglycemia compared with younger participants.
Higher body mass index modifies the relationship between randomized intensive control, achieved glycemic response, and resultant absolute risks of MACE and severe hypoglycemia.
